hero.headline: Trump announces $700 million in funding for coal industry
hero.teaser: The administration is directing nearly $700 million toward coal, including funds from wartime authority.
hero.body:
President Trump announced nearly $700 million in funding for the coal industry during a White House ceremony where he received a trophy from the Washington Coal Club, an advocacy group with ties to the coal industry. Trump described the move as historic action to bring down energy prices and the cost of living for Americans.

The funding package includes $175 million from the Department of Energy allocated to six projects designed to modernize, retrofit and extend the life of coal-fired power plants serving rural and remote communities in West Virginia, Ohio, North Carolina and Kentucky. The remainder comes from wartime authority powers that Trump has directed toward securing long-term power purchase agreements between the Defense Department and coal plants.

At the ceremony, James Grech, CEO of Peabody Energy, the largest coal company in the US, presented Trump with a bronze trophy depicting a coal miner. "We stand here today representing the thousands of coal miners across the country to express our deep gratitude to you, sir, for the actions you have taken to support our industry," Grech said. More than a dozen coal executives and miners attended the event, along with several Republican lawmakers and cabinet members including EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.

Trump signed an executive order directing the Defense Department to purchase power from coal plants for military installations and other mission-critical facilities. "We're going to be buying a lot of coal through the military now," Trump said. "We're lifting up our hard-working American miners like nobody has ever done before."

This announcement represents the latest effort by the Trump administration to revive the US coal industry. In September, the White House announced it would open 13.1 million acres of public land to coal mining and provide $625 million for coal-fired power plants.

Coal has declined significantly as an energy source in the United States over recent decades. According to the Energy Information Administration, US coal production in 2023 was less than half its 2008 level, and coal plants generated only about 15 percent of US electricity in 2024, down from roughly 50 percent in 2000. Coal is considered the most polluting and costly fossil fuel.

Trump has repeatedly expressed support for coal as an energy source throughout his presidency. The award ceremony adds to a series of honors and gifts the president has received from business leaders and officials since the start of his second term, including recognition from FIFA and gifts from Swiss billionaires and Apple's CEO.

cards.headline: Trump nominates Todd Blanche as attorney general
cards.teaser: President Trump said he will nominate acting Attorney General Todd Blanche to permanently lead the Justice Department.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump announced his intention to nominate Todd Blanche as attorney general, moving to make the position permanent. Blanche, Trump's former personal lawyer, currently serves as acting attorney general. If confirmed by the Senate, he would become the administration's top prosecutor.

The nomination will require Senate confirmation, a process expected to present challenges for Blanche given his prior relationship with the president and questions some senators have raised about his qualifications.

cards.headline: Former National Security Advisor John Bolton to plead guilty in classified documents case
cards.body:
John Bolton, the former national security adviser who became a vocal critic of Donald Trump, has agreed to plead guilty to charges related to mishandling classified documents. The plea agreement is subject to court approval, according to sources familiar with the matter.

Bolton will plead guilty to one count of illegal retention of sensitive national security information. The case represents part of what observers describe as an escalating series of prosecutions against Trump's critics.

The investigation came to public attention when FBI agents conducted early morning raids at Bolton's Bethesda, Maryland home and his Washington office on Friday. Bolton was not present at his home when agents arrived, though he was later spotted in the lobby of his office building speaking with FBI personnel. His wife, Gretchen, was seen leaving their home during the search.

Bolton served as Trump's third national security adviser for 17 months, from 2018 to 2019. He departed the administration following disagreements with Trump over Iran, Afghanistan, and North Korea policies. After leaving government service, Bolton wrote a political memoir titled "The Room Where It Happened," which detailed what he characterized as impeachable conduct by Trump. Trump's administration unsuccessfully attempted to block the book's publication, but a judge ruled in June 2020 that it could be released.

The classified documents controversy centers on Bolton's retention of sensitive materials after departing his position. Earlier legal disputes surrounding his memoir similarly involved questions about whether it contained classified information, though those previous actions ultimately proved unsuccessful for the government.

Shortly after the raids became public, FBI Director Kash Patel posted a message on social media stating "NO ONE is above the law." Attorney General Pam Bondi subsequently posted that "America's safety isn't negotiable. Justice will be pursued. Always."

Trump told reporters he was not aware the raid was planned and claimed he did not want to know about such operations. He made critical comments about Bolton, calling him "a real sort of a lowlife" and suggesting he could be "very unpatriotic."

Some observers questioned the timing and motivation behind the investigation. Meghan Hays, a former White House special adviser under Joe Biden, characterized the raid as "extremely political" and "pure revenge." Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi suggested the action may have been designed as a distraction from other ongoing matters.

Bolton had not been detained or charged with crimes at the time of the raids. Trump had previously revoked Bolton's security clearance and canceled his security detail in the early days of his administration this year.

The plea agreement marks a conclusion to the investigation and will require approval from a federal judge before becoming final.

cards.headline: Hezbollah Rejects Cease-Fire Between Israel and Lebanon
cards.teaser: Hezbollah rejected a cease-fire agreement between Israel and the Lebanese government, calling the U.S.-brokered deal a surrender.
cards.body:
Hezbollah rejected a U.S.-brokered cease-fire agreement between Israel and Lebanon announced Wednesday night. The Iran-backed group's leader said the deal amounted to surrender, citing Hezbollah's exclusion from the negotiations that produced the truce.

As a powerful military and political force within Lebanon, Hezbollah's refusal to accept the terms threatens to undermine the agreement's effectiveness. Without the group's cooperation, implementing the cease-fire along the border may prove difficult, potentially leading to continued hostilities between Israel and Lebanon.

cards.headline: House Democrats help Republicans defeat Lebanon war powers resolution
cards.teaser: The majority of House Democrats joined Republicans to defeat a resolution that would have constrained President Trump's authority to wage war in Lebanon.
cards.body:
The majority of House Democrats joined Republicans to defeat a war powers resolution on Lebanon introduced by Rep. Rashida Tlaib. House Democratic leadership opposed the measure, leaving Tlaib and her allies isolated on the issue.

The vote contrasts sharply with the previous day's passage of a similar Iran war powers resolution, which Democratic leadership actively supported. The different outcomes reveal divisions within the Democratic caucus over Middle East policy, with leadership backing constraints on Trump's authority regarding Iran while declining to do the same for Lebanon.

cards.headline: Pentagon may cancel missile sale to Germany over escalation concerns
cards.teaser: Defense officials are reconsidering a planned weapons deployment amid fears of provoking Russia.
cards.body:
The Pentagon is likely to cancel a planned missile sale and deployment to Germany amid concerns about escalating tensions with Russia. This decision reflects a broader reassessment by the United States of the risks involved in providing advanced weapons systems to its allies.

German officials are developing alternative plans to address any resulting deterrence gap. The delayed weapons sales signal a shift in how the U.S. is managing military support to European partners.

cards.headline: Ultra-Orthodox Protesters Riot in Israel Over Military Draft
cards.teaser: Haredim escalate demonstrations against mandatory service as national elections approach.
cards.body:
Ultra-orthodox Jews in Israel rioted in their latest protest against military draft requirements. The Haredim community has intensified demonstrations in recent weeks, with the violence shocking many Israelis.

The protests highlight deepening divisions within Israeli society ahead of national elections. Ultra-orthodox communities have historically received exemptions from military service to pursue religious studies, but efforts to end those exemptions have sparked fierce resistance and underscore broader debates about equality and national obligation.

hero.headline: Marjane Satrapi, Author of Persepolis, Dies at 56
hero.teaser: The Iranian-French writer and illustrator created a graphic novel series that followed a young girl through revolution and war.
hero.body:
Marjane Satrapi, the French-Iranian artist and graphic novelist whose memoir Persepolis reshaped how the world understood Iran, has died at age 56. According to her family, she died of sadness following the death of her husband, Swedish producer Mattias Ripa, who passed away in April of last year.

Satrapi's groundbreaking work told the story of her own childhood and adolescence in Iran during the Islamic Revolution and its aftermath. Published in 2000, Persepolis became an international publishing phenomenon, selling millions of copies and establishing Satrapi as one of the most widely read Iranian authors in the world. The graphic memoir followed a rebellious young girl navigating the upheaval after the Shah's overthrow in 1979 and the establishment of the Islamic Republic, before being sent alone to Europe at age 14.

Born in 1969 in Rasht, Iran, Satrapi was raised in Tehran by her father, an engineer, and her mother, a dress designer. When she was a teenager, her parents sent her to Europe to pursue her education, hoping to protect her from the restrictions of the Islamic Republic. She eventually settled in France, arriving in 1994 and becoming a French citizen in 2006.

In interviews, Satrapi explained that her purpose in creating Persepolis was to help Western readers recognize the humanity of Iranian people. She also wanted to reassure young Iranians that they were being heard and supported by the outside world. When she first created the work, she was an arts student in Strasbourg with limited professional comics experience and never expected it would find a publisher.

The animated film adaptation of Persepolis became an international success, and Satrapi made history as the first woman nominated for the Academy Award for best animated feature. She went on to direct five feature films, including Radioactive in 2019, which starred Rosamund Pike as Marie Curie.

After stepping away from comics for years, Satrapi returned to the medium in 2024 with Woman, Life, Freedom, a collaborative graphic work that brought together 17 Iranian and international comic artists, academics, and researchers. The book examined the protest movement that emerged after the death of Mahsa Amini, a Kurdish-Iranian woman who died in custody in 2022 for allegedly failing to comply with Iran's mandatory headscarf rules.

Throughout her life, Satrapi remained a vocal opponent of Iran's clerical establishment. She believed in the power of drawing as a universal language, stating that it was humanity's first language, preceding even speech.

World leaders and cultural figures paid tribute to her legacy, with President Emmanuel Macron calling her "a great artist who turned her Iranian childhood into a universal tale."

cards.headline: John Bolton to Plead Guilty in Classified Documents Case
cards.teaser: The former Trump national security advisor reached a deal with prosecutors over handling of classified materials.
cards.body:
John Bolton, former national security adviser under President Trump, has reached a plea agreement in a classified documents case. According to sources familiar with the matter, Bolton will plead guilty to one count of illegal retention of sensitive national security information, subject to court approval.

Bolton left Trump's administration and subsequently became a prominent critic of the president, writing a memoir and publicly commenting on his former boss's conduct and policies. The Justice Department filed charges against Bolton in 2025.

cards.headline: Boeing 787 Nose Gear Collapses at Frankfurt Airport, Injuring Workers
cards.teaser: A Lufthansa Dreamliner's front landing gear failed during ground operations, sending several workers to the hospital.
cards.body:
A Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner operated by Lufthansa experienced nose gear collapse at Frankfurt Airport, resulting in injuries to several workers. The aircraft can weigh up to 279 tons at takeoff.

Lufthansa is investigating the cause of the incident, which occurred during ground operations.

cards.headline: Ultra-Orthodox Protesters Riot in Israel Over Military Draft
cards.teaser: Haredim escalate demonstrations against mandatory service as national elections approach.
cards.body:
Ultra-orthodox Jews in Israel rioted in their latest protest against military draft requirements. The Haredim community has intensified demonstrations in recent weeks, with the violence shocking many Israelis.

The protests highlight deepening divisions within Israeli society ahead of national elections. Ultra-orthodox communities have historically received exemptions from military service to pursue religious studies, but efforts to end those exemptions have sparked fierce resistance and underscore broader debates about equality and national obligation.

cards.headline: Sherpa Guide Rescued After Week Missing on Mount Everest
cards.teaser: The climber was found crawling toward base camp after disappearing during an expedition.
cards.body:
Dawa Sherpa was found crawling toward Base Camp six days after going missing at higher altitude on Mount Everest. Cleaners discovered him during their work and helped bring him to safety in what has been described as a remarkable self-rescue.

Sherpas are vital to Himalayan climbing expeditions, handling much of the most dangerous work at extreme altitudes. This rescue underscores the severe hazards guides face on Everest, where sudden weather shifts and the effects of high altitude can quickly become life-threatening.

cards.headline: Hotel Chains Exit Cuba as Trump Tightens Economic Restrictions
cards.teaser: International firms are withdrawing from the island as the administration increases economic pressure.
cards.body:
Major international hotel chains are withdrawing from Cuba following the Trump administration's decision to intensify economic restrictions on the island. The departures mark a sharp reversal from the business expansion that occurred under the Obama administration's more open approach to Cuba.

The Trump administration has implemented a strategy of mounting economic pressure on Cuba through expanded sanctions and limits on U.S. and international business operations. The hotel chain withdrawals suggest this policy approach is achieving its intended outcome.

cards.headline: Senate rejects Democratic effort to block Trump settlement fund
cards.teaser: The Senate voted down an amendment that would have barred President Trump from creating a $1.8 billion fund.
cards.body:
Senate Republicans narrowly blocked a Democratic amendment Thursday that would have prevented President Trump from establishing a $1.8 billion fund to compensate his allies. Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer proposed the language while debating legislation to fund Trump's mass deportation efforts.

The vote revealed fractures within Republican ranks, with three GOP senators joining Democrats in support of the measure. The dispute underscores internal party divisions over the proposed payouts to Trump's political associates.

cards.headline: United Airlines jet was too slow and too low before Newark accident, investigators say
cards.teaser: Federal safety officials said the captain flying a United 767 from Italy misjudged the approach before last month's landing accident.
cards.body:
Original Card Text

The National Transportation Safety Board said the United Airlines Boeing 767 that struck a light pole while landing at Newark Liberty International Airport was traveling too slowly and at too low an altitude. The aircraft was arriving from Italy when the accident occurred.

The impact damaged a truck on the nearby turnpike. Federal investigators are continuing to examine the circumstances that led the captain to fly the aircraft below the proper approach path for landing.

---

Note: The source material provided (NPR and The Guardian articles) confirms the Newark accident story in your original card. The Guardian article about Australia's NDIS is unrelated. Your original card text is accurate and already well-written based on the confirmed facts, so no changes are needed.

cards.headline: Public health agencies face weakened authority after pandemic restrictions
cards.teaser: Some local and state governments have reduced the powers of public health officials following criticism of pandemic-era measures.
cards.body:
Several jurisdictions have reduced the emergency powers of their public health authorities following widespread criticism of pandemic restrictions. The rollback was prompted by public opposition to lockdowns, school closures, mask mandates, and vaccine requirements that were implemented during COVID-19.

Health officials have expressed concern that these diminished powers may limit their ability to respond swiftly to future disease outbreaks. The changes reflect an ongoing tension between public health considerations and individual liberty in how state and local governments approach epidemic response.

cards.headline: Murder trial begins for teenager accused in fatal stabbing at Texas track meet
cards.teaser: Prosecutors said Karmelo Anthony carried out a sneak attack that killed Austin Metcalf at a Frisco school athletic event.
cards.body:
The trial of Karmelo Anthony opened with prosecutors telling jurors that the teenager fatally stabbed Austin Metcalf in an unprovoked assault at a Frisco Independent School District track meet. The prosecution characterized the attack as a surprise assault on the victim.

Jury selection in the case concluded without any Black jurors being seated. The trial is proceeding in a Texas courtroom where attorneys will present evidence about the stabbing that occurred at the school sporting event.

hero.headline: Boeing 787 Nose Gear Collapses at Frankfurt Airport, Injuring Workers
hero.body:
The nose landing gear of a Lufthansa Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner collapsed at Frankfurt Airport, injuring several workers. The German airline said the cause of the accident is under investigation.

The incident involves one of Boeing's wide-body aircraft models, which can weigh up to 279 tons at takeoff. The 787-9 Dreamliner is a long-range aircraft used primarily for international flights. Lufthansa operates multiple aircraft of this type in its fleet.

The collapse occurred while the aircraft was on the ground at Frankfurt Airport, one of Europe's busiest aviation hubs. Workers were injured during the incident, though the airline did not specify the number of injured or the severity of their injuries. The nose gear is a critical component that supports the front portion of the aircraft during ground operations, taxiing, takeoff, and landing.

Boeing has faced increased scrutiny over manufacturing and safety issues in recent years across several aircraft models. The 787 Dreamliner program has previously encountered production quality concerns that resulted in delivery delays and additional inspections. Any incident involving structural failures or landing gear malfunctions raises questions about maintenance procedures, manufacturing quality, and operational safety protocols.

Lufthansa has launched an investigation to determine what caused the landing gear to fail. The inquiry will examine maintenance records, structural integrity, and whether any manufacturing defects contributed to the collapse. Boeing and German aviation authorities are likely to participate in the investigation, which could take weeks or months to complete depending on the complexity of the failure.

cards.headline: Supreme Court Upholds FCC Authority to Fine Cellphone Carriers
cards.teaser: The court sided with the Trump administration in a case over whether telecom companies can demand jury trials when facing fines from the Federal Communications Commission.
cards.body:
The Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that the Federal Communications Commission can impose fines on wireless carriers through its own administrative proceedings without granting companies a jury trial. The decision rejected challenges from AT&T and Verizon, which argued the FCC's in-house penalty system violated their constitutional rights.

The ruling represents a victory for the Trump administration's position on federal regulatory authority. The court affirmed that telecommunications companies can face FCC penalties without the requirement of a jury trial, allowing the agency to continue its enforcement system for regulatory violations.

cards.headline: Lululemon Cuts Annual Forecast Citing Unspecified Business Challenges
cards.teaser: The athletic apparel retailer lowered its full-year outlook and issued weaker second-quarter guidance without disclosing specific reasons for the adjustment.
cards.body:
Lululemon reduced its annual revenue and earnings projections and provided lower guidance for the second quarter. The company cited unspecified headwinds but did not elaborate on what factors are pressuring its business.

The announcement comes as the retailer prepares for a leadership transition with a new CEO. Analysts had previously warned of potential reset risk for fiscal year 2026. Despite the downward revision, Lululemon's stock rose in premarket trading, with some analysts suggesting the valuation appears inexpensive relative to historical levels.

cards.headline: Tata Steel Plant Fire in Wales Causes Major Production Damage
cards.teaser: A large fire at the Port Talbot steelworks resulted in substantial damage to a production line, prompting authorities to advise nearby residents to keep windows and doors closed.
cards.body:
A fire at Tata Steel's facility in Port Talbot, Wales caused significant damage to at least one production line. Local authorities described the blaze and advised residents in surrounding areas to keep their windows and doors closed as emergency crews worked to control the fire.

The Port Talbot plant is one of the largest steelmaking facilities in the United Kingdom. The extent of the damage and the timeline for restoring production capacity remain under assessment. The incident could affect steel output and employment at the site, which has been the subject of ongoing discussions about its future operations.

cards.headline: Dow Gains Over 900 Points as Oil Prices Drop, Tech Stocks Lag
cards.teaser: The Dow Jones Industrial Average surged to a record high while the Nasdaq declined following disappointing earnings from Broadcom.
cards.body:
Original Card Text (Unchanged)

The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed more than 900 points to reach record territory, driven by falling oil prices. The rally reflected investor optimism about easing energy costs, which can reduce inflationary pressures and improve profit margins for many companies.

The Nasdaq declined as technology stocks pulled back following Broadcom's earnings report, which tested investor confidence in artificial intelligence investments. The divergence between the Dow's advance and the Nasdaq's retreat highlighted a rotation away from high-growth tech stocks toward more traditional industrial and financial companies. The drop in oil prices provided relief to sectors sensitive to energy costs.

---

Note: The provided source material does not contain confirmed facts about the specific market movements described in the original card. The Guardian article discusses OpenAI's IPO timing in the broader tech sector, and The Verge content concerns product giveaways—neither directly confirms the Dow gains, oil price movements, Broadcom earnings impact, or Nasdaq performance stated in the original text. Therefore, the original card remains unchanged.

cards.headline: Quantum Computing Firm Quantinuum Goes Public in Oversubscribed Offering
cards.teaser: The Honeywell-backed quantum computing company raised $1.68 billion and began trading on Nasdaq with a valuation of $17.6 billion.
cards.body:
Quantinuum, backed by Honeywell, completed its initial public offering on the Nasdaq with exceptional investor demand. The offering was oversubscribed by a factor of 20 and raised $1.68 billion in an upsized round, valuing the quantum computing company at $17.6 billion.

Shares opened higher on the first day of trading but closed roughly flat. The strong investor interest underscores growing enthusiasm for quantum computing technology, which has the potential to tackle complex computational problems beyond the reach of traditional computers.

cards.headline: Supreme Court Rules SEC Can Collect Illegal Gains Without Proving Victim Losses
cards.teaser: The justices unanimously sided with the Securities and Exchange Commission in a case over the agency's authority to strip wrongdoers of ill-gotten funds.
cards.body:
The Supreme Court unanimously upheld the Securities and Exchange Commission's authority to collect money from securities law violators regardless of whether the agency can identify specific victims or prove they suffered financial losses. The ruling strengthens a critical enforcement tool for the financial watchdog.

The case addressed whether the SEC's disgorgement power—its ability to recover ill-gotten gains—requires demonstrating that identifiable victims lost money equal to the amount collected from wrongdoers. The justices sided with the SEC, affirming the agency can strip wrongdoers of illegal financial gains even without such proof of victim loss.

hero.headline: Fusion startup Helion raises $465 million to build power plant for Microsoft
hero.body:
Helion, a fusion energy company supported by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, has secured $465 million in funding to construct a power plant for Microsoft. The company is targeting 2028 for completion, working to fulfill a commercial agreement with the technology company to supply electricity generated through fusion.

Fusion energy remains largely theoretical in commercial applications, though it has been pursued as a clean energy solution for decades. Helion's approach involves heating plasma to extreme temperatures and using magnetic fields to compress it until fusion reactions occur. Unlike traditional nuclear fission, which splits atoms and generates long-lived radioactive waste, fusion combines atoms and produces no greenhouse gas emissions or hazardous byproducts.

The investment reflects growing interest in fusion technology from major tech companies seeking reliable clean energy sources. Data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure require enormous amounts of electricity, driving companies to explore alternatives to conventional power generation. Microsoft's commitment to purchase power from Helion represents one of the first major commercial agreements for fusion-generated electricity.

The 2028 deadline is aggressive for an industry that has experienced repeated setbacks. Helion has built several prototype machines and announced achieving key technical milestones, but has not yet demonstrated net energy gain, the point at which a fusion reaction produces more energy than is consumed to create it. Other fusion companies and government-funded projects worldwide are pursuing different technological approaches on varying timelines.

The funding will support the power plant's construction and further technology development. Altman has been instrumental in backing Helion, viewing fusion as essential infrastructure for future technological progress. The company's ability to meet its 2028 deadline will serve as a crucial test case for whether private fusion ventures can deliver on their promises to transition the technology from research laboratories to commercial power generation.

Helion operates within a broader landscape of fusion energy investment. Multiple private companies and government programs are racing to commercialize the technology, recognizing its potential to address energy demands while producing minimal environmental impact. The sector has attracted billions in funding from technology leaders and investors confident that fusion will play a central role in powering next-generation infrastructure.

Success would represent a major breakthrough for the energy industry and could reshape how data centers and other power-intensive operations obtain electricity. However, the field faces significant technical challenges, and skeptics question whether fusion can be produced at commercial scale within the timelines companies have announced. Helion's progress toward its 2028 goal will provide important evidence about whether the private fusion sector can deliver on its ambitious promises.

cards.headline: Apple approves first AI agent for Messages for Business platform
cards.teaser: Poke becomes the first AI agent allowed on Apple's Messages for Business, letting users interact with artificial intelligence through text messages.
cards.body:
Apple has approved Poke as the first AI agent on its Messages for Business platform. Poke enables users to interact with artificial intelligence through text messages, bringing automated AI capabilities into Apple's messaging infrastructure for the first time.

This milestone represents a new direction for Messages for Business, which has traditionally connected users with human customer service representatives from companies. The approval of Poke opens the door for AI-powered automation within Apple's messaging ecosystem.

cards.headline: Sun produces three large solar flares within 24 hours
cards.teaser: The sun erupted with three significant solar flares in less than a day, raising the likelihood of northern lights visible across parts of the United States.
cards.body:
The sun has produced three colossal solar flares in less than 24 hours, according to reports from space weather monitoring agencies. The eruptions increase the chances of auroras appearing in the sky across multiple US states.

Solar flares are bursts of electromagnetic radiation from the sun's surface that can affect Earth's magnetic field when directed toward the planet. The flares can trigger geomagnetic storms that produce colorful auroras, typically visible near the poles but sometimes extending to lower latitudes during strong events. Twenty-three US states may see northern lights as a result of the solar activity.

cards.headline: Bumblebees solve problems using tools in new study
cards.teaser: Scientists found bumblebees can spontaneously use tools to solve problems, demonstrating cognitive abilities previously seen mainly in primates.
cards.body:
Bumblebees can spontaneously solve problems using tools, according to experiments by Finnish scientists. The researchers tested the insects with an adapted version of the classic "box-and-banana" problem—a test developed a century ago to demonstrate that chimpanzees could solve problems by stacking boxes to reach an out-of-reach banana.

The findings reveal that bumblebees possess advanced cognitive abilities despite their tiny brains. The study adds to growing evidence that insects can perform complex problem-solving tasks. Until now, only a select group of species—including various primates, elephants, and crows—had been known to demonstrate this level of insight and spontaneous problem-solving ability.

cards.headline: Meta builds data centers in tents to reduce costs
cards.teaser: Meta has adopted a tactic previously used by Tesla, constructing data centers in tents as a way to slash its massive infrastructure spending.
cards.body:
Meta is building data centers in tents, borrowing a cost-cutting strategy from Tesla. The approach represents one way the company aims to reduce its massive data center bill as it expands infrastructure to support artificial intelligence and other computing needs.

Data centers typically require permanent buildings with specialized cooling, power systems, and security features. The tent-based approach suggests Meta is seeking faster deployment and lower construction costs, though technical details about how the temporary structures handle the demanding requirements of data center operations were not provided.

cards.headline: Elon Musk seeks to end FTC audits of X data handling
cards.teaser: Musk has made another attempt to escape Federal Trade Commission audits of how X handles user data, despite warnings from public commenters.
cards.body:
Elon Musk is making another attempt to escape Federal Trade Commission audits of X's data handling practices. The move comes as public commenters have warned the FTC that Musk cannot be trusted to protect X user privacy.

The FTC has been monitoring X, formerly Twitter, following concerns about the company's data security and privacy practices. Musk has previously objected to the agency's oversight, arguing the audits are burdensome. The latest effort to end the audits continues a pattern of resistance to regulatory scrutiny of the social media platform.

cards.headline: Cable industry warns FCC that foreign router ban could cause disruptions
cards.teaser: The cable lobby is seeking a waiver from FCC rules banning foreign-made routers, citing shortages of memory and substrate components.
cards.body:
The NCTA cable lobby has warned the Federal Communications Commission that enforcing a ban on foreign routers could lead to disruptions. The industry group is seeking a waiver from the rule, citing shortages of memory and substrate materials used in router manufacturing.

The FCC has implemented restrictions on certain foreign equipment in telecommunications networks due to security concerns. The cable industry argues that component shortages make compliance with the ban difficult, potentially affecting their ability to maintain and expand network infrastructure.

hero.headline: Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin requests trade from Detroit
hero.body:
Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin has requested a trade from Detroit, sources told ESPN on Thursday. The move marks a significant development for the franchise, as Larkin has served as team captain and been a cornerstone of the organization.

Larkin's trade request comes as the Red Wings continue their rebuilding process. The team has struggled in recent seasons to return to playoff contention after years of dominance in the late 1990s and 2000s. As captain, Larkin had been expected to lead the franchise through its transition period.

The 28-year-old center has been with Detroit since being drafted in 2014. He was named the 37th captain in franchise history in January 2021, taking over a role previously held by franchise legends. His decision to request a trade represents a turning point for both his career and the organization's direction.

The trade request puts Detroit's front office in a difficult position. Trading a team captain mid-rebuild can accelerate a roster overhaul but also sends a message about the timeline for competitive success. The organization will need to weigh whether to honor Larkin's request or attempt to convince him to remain with assurances about the team's future direction.

For Larkin, the request suggests a desire to compete for a Stanley Cup sooner than Detroit's current trajectory might allow. As a captain requesting a trade, he joins a small group of franchise players who have sought exits from their teams. The Red Wings now face questions about their rebuilding strategy and what return they might receive if they choose to move their captain.

cards.headline: NBA issues lifetime bans to fans who disrupted Finals for selfie
cards.teaser: Two fans received lifetime bans from all NBA arenas after a selfie-seeking incident during Game 1 of the NBA Finals.
cards.body:
Two fans received lifetime bans from all NBA arenas after running onto the court during Game 1 of the NBA Finals on Wednesday night to take a selfie with San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama. The league confirmed the penalties Thursday.

The incident prompted the NBA to examine fan conduct more broadly. The league is also investigating a separate incident from the same game involving New York Knicks guard Jalen Brunson, who appeared upset after an interaction with fans during the fourth quarter of his team's 105-95 victory.

cards.headline: NBA investigating interaction between Jalen Brunson and courtside fans
cards.teaser: The league is looking into an interaction between Knicks star Jalen Brunson and courtside fans late in Game 1 of the NBA Finals.
cards.body:
The NBA is investigating an incident involving Knicks star Jalen Brunson and courtside fans during the fourth quarter of Game 1 of the NBA Finals on Wednesday night. Brunson appeared upset following the interaction during New York's 105-95 victory over the San Antonio Spurs.

The league opened its investigation after the game concluded. In a separate incident from the same Finals opener, two fans received lifetime bans from all NBA arenas after running onto the court to take a selfie with Spurs player Victor Wembanyama.

cards.headline: Packers sign Christian Watson to four-year, $110.5 million extension
cards.teaser: Wide receiver Christian Watson and the Packers agreed to a four-year contract extension worth $110.5 million with a $31 million signing bonus.
cards.body:
Wide receiver Christian Watson and the Green Bay Packers agreed to a four-year contract extension worth $110.5 million on Thursday, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter. The deal includes a $31 million signing bonus and keeps Watson with the team through the 2030 season.

The extension places Watson among the NFL's highest-paid receivers and reflects the Packers' investment in their passing game ahead of the upcoming season.

cards.headline: Liverpool appoints Andoni Iraola as new head coach
cards.teaser: Liverpool confirmed the hiring of Andoni Iraola as their new head coach, replacing Arne Slot.
cards.body:
Liverpool have appointed Andoni Iraola as their new head coach on a two-year contract. The 43-year-old Spaniard replaces Arne Slot, who was sacked just six days before the announcement.

Iraola arrives from Bournemouth, where he worked with Liverpool's sporting director Richard Hughes. Liverpool moved quickly to secure their preferred candidate, who was identified as ideal for their playing style. Other clubs including Milan, Bayer Leverkusen and Crystal Palace had also pursued the Basque coach.

cards.headline: Russian teen Mirra Andreeva advances to French Open final
cards.teaser: Mirra Andreeva reached her first Grand Slam final by defeating Marta Kostyuk and will face qualifier Maja Chwalinska for the French Open title.
cards.body:
Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva advanced to her first Grand Slam final by defeating Ukraine's Marta Kostyuk at the French Open. Andreeva dominated the semifinal matchup, showcasing strong play throughout the contest.

She will face qualifier Maja Chwalinska in the championship match. Chwalinska earned her spot in the final through an impressive qualifying run, defeating Diana Shnaider 7-6, 6-4 in the other semifinal.

cards.headline: White House task force calls World Cup security challenge unprecedented
cards.teaser: Andrew Giuliani says this summer's World Cup poses an unprecedented security challenge due to its size and scope.
cards.body:
This summer's World Cup will present an unprecedented security challenge because of its massive scale, according to Andrew Giuliani, executive director of the White House FIFA World Cup 2026 Task Force. The tournament will be the largest sporting event ever hosted in the United States.

Law enforcement agencies across federal, state, and local levels are actively coordinating their response to secure venues and protect attendees. The multi-city format of the tournament requires extensive collaboration among different authorities to manage security effectively.

hero.headline: Marjane Satrapi, Author of Persepolis, Dies at 56
hero.body:
Marjane Satrapi, the French-Iranian artist and graphic novelist whose acclaimed memoir Persepolis transformed international perceptions of Iran, has died at age 56. Her family said she "died of sadness" following the death of her husband, Swedish producer Mattias Ripa, who passed away on April 8 the previous year.

Satrapi was born in 1969 in Rasht, Iran, near the Caspian Sea, and grew up in Tehran with her father, an engineer, and her mother, a dress designer. As a teenager, her parents sent her to Europe to continue her education and shield her from the restrictions of the Islamic Republic. She eventually settled in France, arriving in 1994 and becoming a French citizen in 2006.

In 2000, while still an arts student in Strasbourg with limited professional comics experience, Satrapi published Persepolis. The graphic memoir chronicled her childhood during Iran's Islamic Revolution and her teenage years in Europe. She initially had modest expectations, telling El País in 2020: "I didn't even think I'd find a publisher. I thought I'd make 50 photocopies for my friends to read." The book became a global publishing phenomenon, selling millions of copies and establishing her as one of the world's most widely read Iranian authors.

Satrapi later co-directed an animated film adaptation of Persepolis, which became an international success and made her the first woman nominated for an Academy Award for Best Animated Feature. Discussing her choice of medium, she explained in a 2012 interview that "drawing is the first language of human beings, before writing, before even talking, before words."

Beyond Persepolis, Satrapi directed five feature films, including Radioactive, a 2019 biographical drama about Marie Curie starring Rosamund Pike. She was also a vocal opponent of Iran's clerical government throughout her life. In 2024, she returned to comics by coordinating Woman, Life, Freedom, a collaborative graphic work featuring 17 Iranian and international artists exploring the protest movement that followed the 2022 death of Mahsa Amini in police custody.

Satrapi described the purpose of her work as reassuring young Iranians they were heard and supported globally. She told the Guardian in 2024 that Persepolis aimed to make Western readers recognize the humanity of Iranian people, showing "they're actually human beings like us."

Tributes poured in from French political and cultural figures. President Emmanuel Macron called her "a great artist who turned her Iranian childhood into a universal tale." Author Margaret Atwood noted that while she had written about the repression of women in theocratic regimes, "Marjane Satrapi lived it."

Satrapi's work continues to be taught in schools and universities worldwide, introducing new generations to the complexities of life in Iran and the immigrant experience.

cards.headline: CBS Fires Three 60 Minutes Correspondents
cards.teaser: The network dismissed three correspondents from its flagship news program, sparking responses from television personalities and industry figures.
cards.body:
CBS News terminated three correspondents from 60 Minutes this week: Scott Pelley, Sharyn Alfonsi, and Cecilia Vega. Anderson Cooper had previously announced his departure in February. The firings mark a significant upheaval for the program, which has been the most-watched news show for 52 consecutive seasons.

Pelley accused CBS executives of instructing him to inject falsehoods and bias into his reporting. The new leadership under Bari Weiss has prompted concern among staff about whether the show can continue production for its 59th season in September, with questions about which of the remaining correspondents will stay.

cards.headline: Starz Greenlights Power: Legacy Series
cards.teaser: The network ordered eight episodes of a new Power sequel reuniting two characters from previous installments of the franchise.
cards.body:
Starz has greenlit Power: Legacy, a new series in the Power franchise. The show will follow Tommy Egan, played by Joseph Sikora, and Tariq St. Patrick, played by Michael Rainey Jr., the son of Tommy's late friend James Ghost St. Patrick. Starz ordered eight episodes for the first season.

Both actors previously led their own separate Power spinoff series. The reunion marks the first time the two characters will share a series since earlier installments of the franchise. Variety confirmed the greenlight.

cards.headline: Bill Ackman Sells $290.5 Million in Universal Music Stock
cards.teaser: The record company is repurchasing shares from the billionaire investor's fund after rejecting a takeover proposal.
cards.body:
Universal Music announced it will repurchase over 14.2 million shares from Pershing Square, the capital fund founded by billionaire investor Bill Ackman. The buyback is valued at approximately $290.5 million, or 250 million euros.

The repurchase follows Universal Music's rejection of a takeover proposal from Pershing Square. Universal Music is the world's largest record company. The transaction reduces Ackman's stake in the company after his unsuccessful acquisition attempt.

cards.headline: Advance Tickets for The Odyssey Film Overwhelm AMC Systems
cards.teaser: Wait times for purchasing tickets to the upcoming film initially reached one hour before dropping as demand surged.
cards.body:
Ticket sales for The Odyssey overwhelmed AMC's website and app, generating wait times that initially reached one hour before dropping to eight minutes. The film generated what multiple outlets described as epic demand from fans rushing to purchase advance tickets.

AMC announced that The Odyssey will play a three-week run at the Westwood Village Theatre in 70mm format. Buyers reported encountering multiple error messages while attempting to purchase IMAX tickets. The Los Angeles Times described the ticket demand as slamming the theater chain's website.

cards.headline: Dateline to Air Luigi Mangione Investigation Special
cards.teaser: The news program will examine the case in a special airing Friday night at 10 p.m. ET.
cards.body:
Dateline will air a special investigation into Luigi Mangione on Friday, June 5, at 10 p.m. ET. The program promises to dive deeper into the Mangione investigation.

The special's description states that people use Mangione as a Rorschach test, suggesting the case has generated varied interpretations. The broadcast represents Dateline's examination of the mystery surrounding the case.

cards.headline: Sara Bareilles Documentary Good Grief Premieres at Tribeca
cards.teaser: The film chronicles the singer-songwriter's album about loss and features commentary from director Josh Alexander.
cards.body:
Sara Bareilles: Good Grief is premiering at the Tribeca Film Festival. The documentary follows singer-songwriter Sara Bareilles as she created her album of the same name, which explores themes of loss and grief. Director Josh Alexander helmed the project, collaborating with Bareilles to document the album's creation.

The film's title reinterprets the common phrase "good grief" in a literal way, transforming what might seem like an oxymoron into something meaningful. The documentary captures how Bareilles channeled loss into her music, turning personal grief into artistic expression.

hero.headline: Trump announces $700 million in funding for coal industry
hero.teaser: The administration is directing nearly $700 million toward coal, including funds from wartime authority.
hero.body:
President Trump announced nearly $700 million in funding for the coal industry during a White House ceremony where he received a trophy from the Washington Coal Club, an advocacy group with ties to the coal industry. Trump described the move as historic action to bring down energy prices and the cost of living for Americans.

The funding package includes $175 million from the Department of Energy allocated to six projects designed to modernize, retrofit and extend the life of coal-fired power plants serving rural and remote communities in West Virginia, Ohio, North Carolina and Kentucky. The remainder comes from wartime authority powers that Trump has directed toward securing long-term power purchase agreements between the Defense Department and coal plants.

At the ceremony, James Grech, CEO of Peabody Energy, the largest coal company in the US, presented Trump with a bronze trophy depicting a coal miner. "We stand here today representing the thousands of coal miners across the country to express our deep gratitude to you, sir, for the actions you have taken to support our industry," Grech said. More than a dozen coal executives and miners attended the event, along with several Republican lawmakers and cabinet members including EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.

Trump signed an executive order directing the Defense Department to purchase power from coal plants for military installations and other mission-critical facilities. "We're going to be buying a lot of coal through the military now," Trump said. "We're lifting up our hard-working American miners like nobody has ever done before."

This announcement represents the latest effort by the Trump administration to revive the US coal industry. In September, the White House announced it would open 13.1 million acres of public land to coal mining and provide $625 million for coal-fired power plants.

Coal has declined significantly as an energy source in the United States over recent decades. According to the Energy Information Administration, US coal production in 2023 was less than half its 2008 level, and coal plants generated only about 15 percent of US electricity in 2024, down from roughly 50 percent in 2000. Coal is considered the most polluting and costly fossil fuel.

Trump has repeatedly expressed support for coal as an energy source throughout his presidency. The award ceremony adds to a series of honors and gifts the president has received from business leaders and officials since the start of his second term, including recognition from FIFA and gifts from Swiss billionaires and Apple's CEO.

cards.headline: House Democrats help Republicans defeat Lebanon war powers resolution
cards.teaser: The majority of House Democrats joined Republicans to defeat a resolution that would have constrained President Trump's authority to wage war in Lebanon.
cards.body:
The majority of House Democrats joined Republicans to defeat a war powers resolution on Lebanon introduced by Rep. Rashida Tlaib. House Democratic leadership opposed the measure, leaving Tlaib and her allies isolated on the issue.

The vote contrasts sharply with the previous day's passage of a similar Iran war powers resolution, which Democratic leadership actively supported. The different outcomes reveal divisions within the Democratic caucus over Middle East policy, with leadership backing constraints on Trump's authority regarding Iran while declining to do the same for Lebanon.

cards.headline: Trump says Bill Pulte will serve as temporary intelligence director
cards.teaser: The president clarified that his pick for national intelligence chief would not be permanent amid bipartisan pushback.
cards.body:
President Trump announced Thursday that Bill Pulte, his choice for director of national intelligence, would serve only temporarily in the role. The appointment has faced criticism from both Democrats and Republicans.

Trump defended Pulte's credentials, describing him as intelligent and having high integrity. Pulte currently leads the Federal Housing Finance Agency. By characterizing the position as temporary, Trump appears to be addressing concerns about assigning a housing official to oversee the nation's intelligence operations.

cards.headline: House panel releases transcript of Pam Bondi interview on Epstein files
cards.teaser: The former attorney general declined to answer many questions and pointed to acting AG Todd Blanche.
cards.body:
The House Oversight and Government Reform Committee released the transcript from its closed-door meeting with former Attorney General Pam Bondi. The roughly four-hour session shows Bondi declining to answer numerous questions about the handling of the Epstein files.

Bondi directed responsibility toward acting Attorney General Todd Blanche when pressed on the matter. The transcript reveals limited cooperation from the former attorney general during the committee's investigation.

cards.headline: Deb Haaland wins New Mexico Democratic primary for governor
cards.teaser: The former Biden administration official could become the first female Native American governor.
cards.body: Deb Haaland won the Democratic nomination for New Mexico's gubernatorial race and will advance to the general election. The former Biden administration official could make history as the first female Native American governor if elected in November.

cards.headline: Hilton and Becerra lead in California governor primary
cards.teaser: Republicans Steve Hilton and Chad Bianco face Democrats Xavier Becerra, Katie Porter, and Tom Steyer in the race to replace Gavin Newsom.
cards.body:
Steve Hilton narrowly leads the California governor's race, with former US health and human services secretary Xavier Becerra in close second place, according to polling data. Billionaire Tom Steyer trails both candidates. Under California's primary system, the top two vote-getters will advance to the general election.

State election officials are continuing to count uncounted primary ballots, a process that could take days or weeks to complete. The race remains unsettled as voters await final results.

cards.headline: Susan Collins breaks with GOP on insurance company investigation amendment
cards.teaser: The Maine senator voted for a Democratic amendment to investigate insurers denying medical care.
cards.body:
Sen. Susan Collins voted Thursday with Democrats on an amendment to send the $70 billion budget reconciliation package to the Judiciary Committee for an investigation into insurance companies denying medical care to patients. The vote put her at odds with Senate Republican leaders.

Collins, a vulnerable Republican facing reelection, supported the Democratic amendment that would examine what the party characterized as insurance company abuses.
